methodology.title: Curated source-first AI intelligence brief
methodology.summary: This dataset is generated from public source feeds. Items are linked back to their original URLs, timestamped, and auto-categorized for triage rather than treated as infallible truth.
caveats: Feed freshness depends on source publication latency and RSS availability.
Threads coverage uses RSSHub adapters and may fail or lag if the upstream route changes.
Automatic categorization is heuristic and should be reviewed for decision-critical workflows.

research.title: Optimal Linear Regression Without a Variance
research.summary:
We study high-probability linear regression in the infinite variance regime, wherecthe regression noise has only a finite conditional $α$-moment $ν$ for some unknown $α\in(1,2)$, and the covariates may only have finite moments up to a given order (e.g., 4th moment). We give a black-box reduction that converts finite-variance regression procedures into weak-moment procedures. The reduction is based on empirical residual pruning and is agnostic to the moment exponent, the noise scale, the covariance, and the design moment. Under a finite fourth-moment condition on the covariates, any finite-variance subroutine attaining the sub-Gaussian rate yields the following when the number of samples $n$ is above a suitably defined threshold: Without knowing $α$ or $ν$, we have with probability at least $1-δ$ that $ \|\widehatθ-θ^*\|_Σ
  \lesssim_α
  ν^{1/α}
  \big(\frac{d+\log(1/δ)}{n}\big)^{\frac{α-1}α}, $ where $d$ is the dimension, $Σ$ is the covariate covariance matrix, and $\|v\|_Σ:=(v^\topΣv)^{1/2}$. We further prove a matching minimax lower bound that holds under the same conditions. The reduction is computationally efficient whenever the finite-variance subroutine is. We also obtain a distribution-free prediction guarantee under a bounded raw $α$-moment assumption on the response, and give an analogous $α$-agnostic reduction for mean estimation.

research.title: A Methodologically Rigorous Benchmark of Linear Regression,RNN, and LSTM for S&P 500 Forecasting:Identifying Sources of Performance Inflation in Financial DeepLearning
research.summary: This study examines one-day-ahead forecasting of the S&P 500 closing level using a 2006-2025 dataset that includes fundamental price data, macroeconomic indicators, and engineered technical features. We benchmark three model families, namely linear regression, vanilla recurrent neural networks (RNN), and long short-term memory networks (LSTM), within a unified preprocessing and chronological evaluation pipeline. A central contribution of this work is a methodological audit of common practices in the deep-learning-for-stock-prediction literature. We identify three sources of result inflation that frequently appear in published methodologies: wavelet-denoised evaluation targets, the absence of a naive persistence baseline, and best-of-N replicate reporting. We then re-evaluate all model families under a corrected protocol that controls for each. Performance is reported using root mean squared error, mean absolute percentage error, and the Pearson correlation coefficient, averaged across N = 30 independent replicates per configuration. We compare models on accuracy, stability across replicates, and architectural depth sensitivity, using the naive persistence forecast (predicting today's close as tomorrow's close) as a primary baseline against which all candidate models must demonstrate improvement.

research.title: MemOnce: A Scalable Memory Architecture for Large Language Models
research.summary: Deploying large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon and continual interactions requires maintaining reusable memory states for future inference, posing challenges for existing architectures. Standard Transformers accumulate layer-wise, token-level KV caches, incurring linear GPU memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as the context expands. In contrast, linear-time architectures compress history into fixed-size states, but struggle to retain fine-grained details. We introduce MemOnce, a foundation architecture that learns scalable memory states for language models. MemOnce is based on two core designs: (a) Memory encoder-decoder: it caches only a small subset of final-layer hidden states as compact memory representations and dynamically decodes them back into KV caches for attention layers; (b) Memory sparse attention: for each continual input, MemOnce adaptively retrieves relevant memory representations, with the sparse indices computed only once across layers. Coupling these two designs enables efficient on-the-fly memory loading and KV cache decoding, drastically reducing the GPU memory footprint and achieving linear-time complexity. We conduct extensive experiments to show that MemOnce outperforms Transformers and other architectures across varying model sizes, context lengths, and training paradigms (pretraining and post-training adaptation). In particular, adapting Qwen3.5-4B with MemOnce reduces memory state cache by 1313$\times$ and prefill latency by 6.9$\times$ at 1M context, and improves throughput by 3.5$\times$ and overall memory performance by +5.77%. Finally, MemOnce generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks, achieving competitive results against specialized models.

research.title: On the Complete Feature Set for ADHD Classification in Children and Adolescents Based on EEG Signals
research.summary: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition that can affect attention, activity and impulse control. Electroencephalography (EEG) records brain activity as children and adolescents perform cognitive tasks. However, comparing features derived from these recordings requires consistent signal preparation, shared analysis windows and documented quality decisions. We curated 669 existing BALLADEER recordings from 156 participants across five task conditions so that researchers can compare seven EEG feature families on the same time intervals for each participant and task. The dataset links continuous signals to precomputed measurements from 115 feature definitions or templates and records the quality decisions made for each recording. Analyses must still account for repeated measurements within participants, residual artefacts and differences between acquisition systems. Technical validation covered signal integrity, numerical checks on feature estimators and completeness of the released files. In every task, the median proportion of recording time retained after preprocessing was 100%. To illustrate reuse, we report saved participant-held-out evaluations comparing XGBoost using all seven families on eight-second windows with a predictor based only on recruitment-group prevalence in the training fold. Recruitment-group discrimination was stronger in Robots than in the three Slackline conditions. These descriptive results from overlapping cohorts do not establish diagnostic validity. The dataset, curation software and aggregate results for the predictive example are publicly available.

research.title: Non-penetrating World Models
research.summary: We study a new problem of preventing object penetration in interactive video world models. To understand how existing models handle this, we introduce NoPeBench, a benchmark that evaluates how world models respond to physical obstacles. Our evaluation reveals that none of the open-source models can reliably prevent such failures. Surprisingly, however, these models already encode the information needed to predict such violations. We find that the hidden states of diffusion transformers (DiTs) can predict whether a candidate action will penetrate an obstacle. Building on this, we introduce NoPeWorld, a lightweight framework that detects and prevents penetration. Specifically, we train a small prediction head on top of a frozen DiT's hidden states to read out if a candidate action is safe or not. Unsafe actions are then replaced with safe ones that best preserve the original intent. Despite its simplicity, NoPeWorld substantially reduces the physical violation rate, averaged over six video world models, from 74% to 16%. Remarkably, our method shows zero-shot generalization to open-domain imagery, third-person viewpoints, and moving obstacles. We publicly release our code, the NoPeBench benchmark, and model weights. Project Page: https://nopeworld.github.io .

research.title: Model Carving: Training Transformers That Optimize Their Own Topology
research.summary: Machine learning has largely kept separate the choice of architecture and the process of training. A classic Transformer, for instance, trains a fixed set of attention and MLP sublayers at every layer, in the same order, and optimizes the weights within. This uniformity is a convention rather than a principled design choice, and it is likely suboptimal: the best architecture for a given task may be smaller, more efficient, and far from uniform. We believe that, ideally, training itself should shape the model's topology. To this end, we introduce Model Carving, which learns both a Transformer's weights and its architecture in a single run. By applying learnable, scalar gates to each sublayer, we allow the training loss to remove the model's own components during training -- freeing a smaller heterogeneous network inside. We evaluate Model Carving by pre-training standard Transformers from 140M to 2.7B parameters and looped Transformers from 140M to 1.3B. At equal training compute, carved models reach a lower validation loss than dense models trained with up to 1.7 times more compute. Furthermore, carved models also outperform size-matched models produced by pruning or distillation, suggesting that the best way to obtain small models for edge devices is to carve them during training, not to compress a large one afterwards. This advantage both grows with scale and carries over to downstream tasks such as few-shot evaluation and generation. Because the removed sublayers no longer run, carved models also cost up to 34% fewer FLOPs per token and decode up to 1.6 times faster without cost in quality. Our results show that architecture, like weights, should be learned and not fixed in advance, and that inside every large transformer is a smaller, faster, stronger one waiting to be carved out.

research.title: Ranking-Preserving Coreset Selection for Efficient Evolutionary Hyperparameter Optimization
research.summary: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) is essential for high predictive performance, but its computational cost becomes prohibitive when candidate configurations require repeated training on large datasets. This paper proposes a ranking-preserving coreset (RPC) selection framework for accelerating evolutionary HPO. The method constructs a compact coreset that preserves the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations observed on the full training data. Coreset selection is formulated as an evolutionary optimization problem that maximizes Spearman rank correlation between full-data and subset-based configuration rankings while penalizing subset size. The selected coreset is then used for HPO with three evolutionary algorithms: Genetic Algorithm (GA), Cross-generational elitist Selection, Heterogeneous Recombination and Cataclysmic Mutation (CHC), and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). Experiments on seven tabular, two text, and two image benchmark datasets show that RPC substantially reduces HPO time while maintaining test accuracy comparable to full-dataset HPO across decision tree, text classification, and image classification tasks. Across datasets and optimizers, HPO-stage speedups range from approximately 1.14x to 8.80x, while the one-time coreset construction cost is accounted for separately through end-to-end runtime and break-even analysis. On 20 held-out configurations excluded from coreset construction, RPC achieves higher ranking correlation than same-size random sampling on 8 of 11 datasets (dataset-level Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.014). These results show that ranking preservation extends beyond the configurations used during selection. The one-time construction cost can be amortized when the coreset is reused across HPO runs.

research.title: Topology Hub Optimal Transport: Eliminating Long Context Dilution at Flash Speed
research.summary: Long-context models use sparse or structured attention to avoid quadratic cost, yet retrieving a small set of relevant facts embedded among hundreds of thousands of distractors degrades as normalization mass disperses with length. Hub-and-spoke optimal transport (OT) replaces the dense $L \times L$ matrix with a linear-size graph over local windows and $K$ shared hubs balanced by Sinkhorn scaling. Building on block-wise tail refinement and fixed-support transport topology (arXiv:2605.08123, arXiv:2609.07954), we introduce Topology Hub Optimal Transport (THOT): (1) bounded-support capacity gating via simplex sparsemax ($O(L\log L)$) or sorting-free token-local thresholded ReLU ($O(L)$), driving excess distractor mass to zero; (2) a three-sweep $1+2$ annealed row-closed Sinkhorn schedule that damps bipartite residuals; (3) an exact rank-$(D+2R+1)$ One-Reference-Tile adjoint in batched split-factor Triton kernels (BF16 Tensor Cores, FP32 potentials); and (4) a chunked exclusive-prefix causal variant with verified zero future leakage. On NVIDIA L4, sparsemax THOT trained at $L=128$ reaches 97.40% zero-shot recall of fixed bindings at $L=262{,}144$ under pure task loss ($α=0$) and 98.83% at $α=0.05$ (matched by $O(L)$ thresholded ReLU at $α=0.05$, vs. 80.60% at $α=0$), while softmax-gated hub OT drops to 3.52%. In bidirectional operator microbenchmarks, our kernel runs forward+VJP in 100.1 ms at $H=8, D=64, L=262\mathrm{K}$ (2.2x faster with 4.0x smaller compiler temporaries than latent softmax) and 1.34 ms vs. 4.37 ms for cuDNN FlashAttention at $L=4{,}096$; multi-layer LM runs use the unfused path. Zero-shot WikiText-103 multi-needle retrieval hits 100.00% (128/128 queries at $L=65\mathrm{K}$) vs. 0.78% for short-trained RoPE FlashAttention, and compact 4-layer WikiText-4K runs show modest causal and masked LM gains.

research.title: The Optimal Sample Complexity of Agnostic PAC Learning for Partial Concept Classes
research.summary: Let $\mathcal H\subseteq\{-1,+1,\star\}^{\mathcal X}$ be a partial concept class of finite VC dimension $d$. We construct a deterministic agnostic PAC learner that, for every $\varepsilon,δ\in(0,1)$, uses $O((d+\log(1/δ))/\varepsilon^2)$ i.i.d. examples from an arbitrary distribution $\mathcal D$ over $\mathcal X\times\{-1,+1\}$ and returns a total concept $\hat h:\mathcal X\to\{-1,+1\}$ satisfying $\text{er}_{\mathcal D}(\hat h)\leq \min_{h\in\mathcal H}\text{er}_{\mathcal D}(h)+\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-δ$, where $\text{er}_{\mathcal D}(h)=\mathbb P_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal D}[h(x)\neq y]$. This establishes the optimal sample complexity, matching the lower bound of Alon et al. (FOCS 2021).

research.title: BioEmu2: Scalable Emulation of Biomolecular Dynamics
research.summary: Despite major advances in structure prediction, modelling the motions and interactions that drive biomolecular function at scale remains a central challenge. We introduce BioEmu2, a generative model for atomically resolved biomolecular structures combining static structure prediction, equilibrium sampling and time evolution, that samples orders of magnitude faster than molecular dynamics (MD). Trained on experimental and synthetic structures and extensive MD data, it supports multi-component systems containing proteins, nucleic acids, modified residues, ligands and ions. Structure-prediction accuracy is comparable to top open-weight biomolecular folding models, and a context parallel mode enables prediction of megadalton complexes. Equilibrium distributions approximate MD references with free-energy errors near 1 kcal/mol across tested proteins and complexes. Time propagation predicts long-timescale dynamical trajectories and kinetics of binding and conformational changes. Generated structures can be controlled by conditioning on residue contacts or steering with user-defined bias potentials. Enhanced sampling enables free energy calculation involving rare states. BioEmu2 makes the study of biomolecular ensembles and dynamics scalable.

research.title: SUAF: Spectral Universal Advantage Features for Zero-Shot Policy Improvement
research.summary: Reward-independent representations enable reinforcement learning agents to reuse knowledge across tasks, but limited representation capacity raises three fundamental questions: what statistical dependence should these representations capture, which components of that dependence should be retained for policy improvement, and how does discarding the remaining components affect decision-making? We address these questions through canonical dependence analysis. For a reference policy, we construct an action-centered, positive-lag canonical dependence matrix (CDM) that isolates the additional predictive contribution of the current action beyond the current state. Its singular value decomposition yields Spectral Universal Advantage Features (SUAF), paired features that recover delayed advantage through linear reward projections. We show that the spectrum quantifies mutual information between current action and future state-action visitation conditioned on current state and determines reward specific approximation errors. Retaining the leading modes gives optimal rank-constrained approximations under both isotropic average-case and reward-uniform minimax criteria. Separating the immediate reward contrast also avoids the spectral floor arising from direct compression of the full advantage operator. To learn SUAF from reward-free data, we develop an action-centered Soft-HGR objective with bidirectional temporal-difference estimation. We further connect spectral approximation errors to sufficient conditions for policy improvement. Finite-state experiments validate the spectral predictions and feature-learning method, while zero-shot evaluations on discrete tasks and continuous-control benchmarks demonstrate the utility of the learned representations across rewards.

research.title: StereoVLM: Binocular Vision-Language Models for Metric 3D Spatial Reasoning
research.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning. StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy ($δ_1$) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench. Intervention results further indicate that the model's performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors. Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.

news.title: AI-driven technique could help engineers design analog chips faster and with less expense
news.summary: A new technique developed by MIT researchers could help engineers use artificial intelligence to streamline the design and innovation of analog integrated circuits, semiconductor chips that perform vital functions like communication and power management in electronic devices. In the future, this method could allow engineers to prototype faster, explore a wider range of chip designs, and discover new design schemes that might improve the performance and energy efficiency of robots, medical monitors, or industrial sensors. Designing analog integrated circuits that meet specific requirements is usually a cumbersome manual process due to the enormous number of possibilities. Frontier generative AI models have shown success in automating the process, but using these resource-intensive, cloud-hosted models could expose proprietary circuit design and semiconductor foundry data to malicious users. The MIT method, called Small LM Iterating on Circuits, or SLIC (pronounced “slick”), enables engineers to train a small language model to perform analog circuit design as well as or better than a frontier large language model (LLM).  This small model is inexpensive and efficient enough to run on a laptop. Because it’s trained and deployed locally, it can use a company’s circuit design data without raising privacy risks.  When compared to complementary baselines and open-weight frontier LLMs, a small model trained by SLIC more effectively generated designs that achieved the circuit objectives.  “We’ve provided an alternative option to automate analog circuit design. With our technique, engineers can train a small, locally deployable model, using their own confidential data, and then deploy it in their own environment to ensure their assets remain protected,” says Yan Xu, an electrical engineering and computer science (EECS) graduate student and lead author of a paper on this technique. She is joined on the paper by senior author Ruonan Han, a professor of EECS and a member of the MIT Research Laboratory of Electronics; Zhengqi Gao PhD ’26; Wenjie Lu PhD ’18, a former MIT postdoc who is now a principal research scientist at Analog Devices, Inc.; Xin Zhang, a research manager at IBM Research; Duane S. Boning, the Clarence J. LeBel Professor in EECS and MIT vice provost for international activities; and others at IBM Research and Analog Devices. The research will be presented at the 2026 Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems.  “Through some specialized training and area-specific research, we can use much smaller models that consume far fewer resources to achieve almost the same results as flagship models in analog circuit design,” says Han. “This opens many more possibilities in the design of complex chips, especially if we care about costs, data privacy, and customization.” Mimicking human learning Analog integrated circuits enable a device to interact with the physical world. For instance, these circuits boost incoming wireless signals in smartphones and process outputs from sensors that track a car’s engine temperature.  Real-world signals tend to be unpredictable, so engineers must balance a wide and complex array of targets and tradeoffs to maximize analog circuit performance. This has made the design problem especially challenging for AI models. “To design a circuit, engineers find a good starting point based on their intuition and then, drawing on their knowledge of circuit design, tune a few knobs toward the performance they want,” says Xu. “There is no universal way to solve every circuit design problem.” Even if a powerful, cloud-based model could design a circuit as well as a human, most companies would be reluctant to send their foundry-specific data to external AI service providers. With SLIC, the MIT researchers created a training method that teaches a smaller, less expensive, faster language model to design analog integrated circuits that meet user specifications.  The SLIC model uses a few billion parameters, making it several thousand times smaller than frontier models that use trillions of parameters and require enormous amounts of computational resources.  “We tried to mimic the behavior of how a human learns to design a circuit,” Xu says. They used a technique called multi-turn reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where a model works through a multi-step task while adapting to environmental feedback.  When given an analog circuit optimization task, SLIC uses a large LLM to generate several demonstrations of the open source design process. Then SLIC then uses these demonstrations to guide the small model in mimicking this design process.  After the small model gains some initial knowledge about circuit design, SLIC lets it practice by tackling a new design problem on its own. The model makes an initial guess of the design parameters, performs simulations, evaluates the results, and iteratively refines the design using knowledge it gained about analog circuits. Once a design achieves the user’s goals, SLIC prioritizes additional marginal gains. This means the model keeps learning to make improvements that boost performance even when several designs meet the user-defined targets.  An interpretable process Importantly, because SLIC employs models that describe their reasoning using natural language, the user can understand the decisions it makes along the way. “Although the whole process is automated, the user can see what is going on inside the model. This could help the user gain some new ideas about circuit design, and it also adds a lot of confidence about the decision-making process,” Han says. An engineer could utilize SLIC by adapting the researchers’ trained model to their data using a fine-tuning process. Or they could employ the SLIC training process to build their own model with company data, allowing for more customization. “We are seeing an increasing demand for analog chips, but the speed of design has not kept up. This research is trying to bring new capabilities to AI to solve a problem that industry has been stuck on for decades,” Lu says. When the researchers tested SLIC’s ability to design a circuit that met desired performance metrics, their small model came close to matching the performance of the latest GPT model (GPT-6-Astra). It did this while using a fraction of the computational resources.  The researchers also found that the SLIC model maintained its performance when tackling previously unseen circuit structures and adapting to more advanced technology nodes (design and manufacturing rules) and real commercial processes. Because SLIC teaches a model the general chip design process, the system is not tied to any company. This makes it a more scalable approach that could be used by many organizations for a range of circuit applications. “The knowledge the model has gained about circuit design is universal in nature. That is the powerful aspect of this tool,” Han says. In the future, the researchers want to explore self-improving models that can independently learn to handle more diverse topologies and design targets. They also want to use SLIC to build a multi-agent framework, in which many small language models work on different parts of a complex circuit design task. “Yan’s work shows that a locally deployable model can learn transferable design behavior and iterate with a circuit simulator to improve a design, which could reduce repetitive manual tuning for engineers. This is the kind of work the MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab makes possible. We see it as opening the door to more sophisticated custom design, including RF and microwave circuits, in the settings where industry actually works,” says Zhang. This research is funded, in part, by Analog Device, Inc., IBM, and the John L. Ocampo Endowment Fund of MACOM Technology Solutions.

news.title: Q&A: Enabling more human-like interactions and understanding in multimodal foundation models
news.summary: Humans experience and interact with the world through sensory information. This could mean learning correspondences between the sound of bird chirps and the word “robin,” or being able to visually identify and follow your friend “Sarah” in a crowd of people. In many cases, people are able to draw on their latent “multimodal” knowledge — information across multiple data types, from audio to video to text or spoken word — to perform these tasks without many, or sometimes even any, examples. Multimodal foundation models of artificial intelligence are increasingly gaining capabilities that mimic this. However, their apparent multimodal fluency often belies their actual understanding. An MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab team, co-led by Jim Glass, senior research scientist in the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, has been investigating critical failures of state-of-the-art multimodal models and developing benchmarks and data-efficient methods to overcome these performance gaps with limited supervision. He speaks about this work in the following interview. Q:  What were your goals for this project, and why would you opt to address AI models’ weaknesses over scaling to larger models?     A: This project has been going on for many years now, with roughly the same MIT-IBM team of speech and vision experts. We've wanted to explore the relationship between perception (things that you see and hear) and language, largely speaking: We have all of this absorbed knowledge and language skills, text-based, in the form of a large language model, so we wanted to know how you can relate them without using a whole bunch of annotated training data. Sometimes the models have seen certain phenomena, a latent representation of something that they have internally, but maybe due to subsequent fine-tuning or something, it disappears, so, developing techniques to try to make this capability re-emerge is a useful thing.  As you study these publicly available models, you can see weaknesses even in big ones, so I think it's important to try to address these limitations. If you had an unlimited budget, you could go out and create the annotations that you need, but it's also good to be able to try to get these models to learn more on their own. We’ve done that by creating novel benchmarks that we can evaluate against, then developing techniques that perform better on these benchmarks, and getting these models to learn on their own. Throughout our research collaboration — and this has very much been a strong collaboration between MIT and IBM — we have continued to release public benchmarks for people to use, and that's a lasting artifact. I think the overriding themes are multimodalities with language models, trying to address the shortcomings of these models, and trying to develop techniques that do not require a lot of annotated data to complete tasks better. Q:  Can you walk us through how the project has evolved? A: When we first started this project, we were trying to build models that could learn correspondences automatically, not telling the machine anything more than, “This audio caption goes with this picture,” sort of like reading a picture book to a child who's learning language. We would just show it these matching examples, and we'd show it mismatching examples. They could learn that the sequence of sounds that says “lighthouse” corresponds to a picture of a lighthouse, without any text being involved. Moving beyond speech was to include general audio, and then we started looking at video instead of still images. We would train the model, showing it matching video sequences with the corresponding audio stream and then mismatching ones, and make it reconstruct them. We would also mask some of the images or the audio, and have the model reconstruct it. The model would learn strong relationships; then, far beyond speech, it would learn what parrots sound like, or electric guitars versus acoustic guitars, for example. Then, when these large language models started coming out — and this was in the early days, before it had been done by the big companies — we started to learn correspondences between audio and language. Since that time, these large multimodal models have become available, and we've started looking at what some of the limitations of these models are, and are trying to improve upon them with these more or less supervised techniques. Q:  What would you say are some recent highlights of your work? A: Our IPLoc research was looking at the fact that these state-of-the-art models, like GPT-40, can't localize specific objects, given just a few-shot examples. We came up with this technique where we would train it with a pseudonym substitution. There's an example there where we replaced “airplane” with “Elizabeth.” It forces the model to not fall back on things that it had previously learned about and pay more attention to the visual context. Then, we had an audio-based paper, OmniR1 , that was looking at audio-large language models, so these are models that can listen to something and talk about them. One of the disturbing things we found is some of these benchmarks are multiple-choice answers . A lot of times, these models aren't really listening to the sound, but they're almost gaming the question by looking at the answer. What animal is roaring in this audio — like a chipmunk, a lion, an alligator, and a chickadee, or something? It's not even really paying attention to the audio, [but] just going, “Oh, lion.” Part of the reason people do that is that it’s simple to evaluate, whereas if you asked for a text response, you’d somehow have to grade whether it’s accurate. Do you get humans to evaluate it, which can be expensive and time-consuming, or do you use some other language model to be the judge that can have its own set of issues as well? One way to address that is to evaluate these models on a variety of different kinds of benchmarks. We realized you could feed random noise, and they were still doing quite well, which shows that they're just paying attention to the question. So, we tried to develop some methods to have it pay more attention to the audio and minimize this behavior. Q:  Given resource constraints, what is your approach to adapting these large foundation models, and what blend of AI and algorithmic methods do you use that don't require extensive annotated data? A: These days, we can't create one of these very large foundation models ourselves. We don't have the resources to do that, so we're tending to use these available models and trying to adapt them, train them in a weakly supervised way, methods that don't require as much data, like our work on test-time reinforcement learning . Our project was not monolithic, in the sense that we're not all working on one thing. It's more like a thousand flowers bloom, so there's no one particular way that we're approaching things. Q:  In the near future, how do you see multimodal research evolving in your MIT-IBM research team? A: Over the years, we probably produced two dozen or so significant collaborative papers, and during this work, it was amazing to me that the machines could learn these correspondences without being told anything. No one had ever shown that machines could do it before we did that. Some of our early work combining audio with large language models was fun, too: seeing the model talk about what it heard and then having a conversation with it. Now, we are starting to take this for granted, but at the time, it was fun to see. Moving forward, for the coming year, with our MIT-IBM collaboration, we're going to switch gears a little bit and focus more on what's known as full-duplex spoken dialogue systems. These are models that are listening while they’re talking, so it’s more like how humans operate, and this is quite different from what we’ve been doing up until now, which is joint audio-visual work, which we will also continue.  Now, we’ll be focusing on the speech side of things. These full-duplex models have suddenly become an interesting thing to look at, because they would move you away from the rigid turn-taking approach that is used right now when you're talking to some of these models. Ultimately, I think they will be more natural to interact with.  These full-duplex models are just starting to emerge, and some of the ones that are publicly available aren't as good as the big, large language models. They can handle some of these low-level communication skills, but they're still missing some things, like the concept of time, or knowledge depth. So, we're working on trying to address some of these issues. This research has been conducted in coordination with the MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab teams of Rogerio Feris , Brian Kingsbury , and Samuel Thomas of IBM Research, and Hilde Kuehne of the University of Tuebingen, who is an MIT-IBM affiliated researche r.
authors: Lauren Hinkel | MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab

news.title: New approach enables physically consistent AI models of chaotic systems
news.summary: Modeling of complex, chaotic processes such as weather and climate patterns and turbulent flows in aviation or in ocean currents has advanced enormously in recent years. However, such models are still prone to drift into physically impossible predictions over time. Now, researchers with MIT’s Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS) have found a way to introduce physics-based restrictions on machine learning models that can ensure that such models never exceed realistic bounds, based on what is actually possible in the real world. This new approach, using information that is now being made freely available by the team, could significantly improve the usefulness and reliability of such models, which besides climate and weather are also used in a wide range of industrial processes, aeronautics, and hydrology. The new findings are published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) in a paper by MIT graduate student Sunbochen Tang and MIT professors Navid Azizan and Themistoklis Sapsis.  “Lack of guarantees for a bounded response has always been a major obstacle on formulating data-driven models for complex nonlinear systems,” says Sapsis, a professor of mechanical engineering and LIDS affiliate. The approach the team has developed, he says, “paves the way for applying the most advanced machine-learning architectures for prediction and control in a plethora of real-world problems, even those characterized by intrinsic instabilities.” Developing reliable models for complex dynamical systems is important across many domains. In fluid dynamics, turbulent flows can disrupt air travel, reduce the efficiency of wind turbines, and affect fuel economy of vehicles. Similarly, in weather forecasting, the chaotic nature of atmospheric dynamics makes accurate long-term predictions difficult.  “Tiny differences in the starting conditions can lead to dramatically different outcomes in a chaotic system,” Azizan says. “That makes predicting its behavior far into the future extremely difficult.” And yet, there are always physical constraints on the kinds of changes that are possible in the real world. “Chaos does not mean anything can happen. These systems often remain bounded, and their models should, too.” But how to introduce those boundaries into the models has been a thorny problem, says Azizan, the Hayes Associate Professor in the Department of Mechanical Engineering and the Institute for Data, Systems, and Society, and a principal investigator in LIDS. “A model can match the data over a short period and still fail when you let it run for a long time,” he says. “Small errors can accumulate until the simulation produces values that grow without limit,” producing predictions that could never actually occur in real systems. “It’s a fundamental problem with many of the existing machine learning models,” he says. “It’s a question that comes up frequently in different domains: how can we embed physical constraints into these models in a way that preserves their flexibility, but ensures physically meaningful outputs?” “We want to preserve the chaos without the artificial runaway behavior that the real system does not have,” he says. “Our approach gives the model room to learn complex dynamics while guaranteeing that its trajectories stay bounded.” This is the first work that establishes such formal guarantees for machine learning models of chaos. Previous attempts to prevent unrealistic results from such models have often been based on “imposing penalties or incentives during training,” says Tang, a doctoral student in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and LIDS, using functions that are often designed based on privileged information about the system. But as these only apply during the training process for the model, “there’s no guarantee that the model will satisfy the underlying constraints intended by such incentives at test time” once it is dealing with new inputs when it is actually used. “The model could still produce unbounded predictions,” he says. To illustrate why simply imposing arbitrary limits would not be a satisfactory solution to the prediction stability issue, Tang explains, “you can cap the predictions, for example, by setting an arbitrary limit on physical quantities, such as 100 degrees for temperature. That’s one possible way to keep predictions bounded, but it could restrict the model from representing complex and nontrivial features that should be learned directly from the data.” He says that “what sets our approach apart is that we formulate energy-based constraints. We let the model learn an energy-like function,” based on real-world chaotic systems, where energy dissipation helps keep trajectories bounded despite their complex behaviors. “Specifically, the model learns an energy-like function, along with a boundary where its chaotic behavior should be confined to. We then add a projection layer, a component that adjusts how the model predicts the system will evolve, to enforce energy dissipation as a hard constraint. Outside this boundary, the energy-like quantity must decrease, so the simulated system is drawn toward the bounded region. That way, we can establish theoretical guarantees that the model prediction remains bounded over arbitrarily long forecast windows.” The team tested their approach on a variety of different well-known physical systems, ranging from simple textbook cases to highly complex multidimensional systems, and found that their approach closely matched the true outcomes, while conventional approaches soon deviated into impossible predictions. Azizan adds that “the fundamental difference between our approach and the existing approaches is what we call hard constraining versus soft constraining.” While many of the current approaches “try to incentivize the model to satisfy the constraints, they’re not treated as hard constraints. Our approach is based on the concept of hard-constrained neural networks,” so that what comes out “is always physically consistent, even if it’s a completely new case the model hasn’t seen.” “AI models shine in scenarios where there’s a large amount of data available,” Azizan says, for example with images or with text, both of which are abundantly available on the internet. However, he says, “for a lot of physical systems, data is not as abundant.” For such cases where the data is limited, he says, “these physics-constrained approaches can help a lot, because the physics of the problem is another source of information.” The new approach is broadly useful for any chaotic systems. “This is readily applicable to a wide range of neural network architectures,” Tang says. They plan to continue testing it on ever-larger systems. “We’re trying to see how well this would work on data-driven models of realistic weather systems.” “The projection layer is modular: it is model-agnostic and can work with different neural network architectures,” Azizan says. “We hope other researchers and practitioners will build on it and test it on larger and even more complex problems.” The paper, along with open-source code, is now accessible online at PNAS . A follow-up work this year by members of the team was presented at the Learning for Dynamics and Control conference. The paper won the conference’s Best Paper Award. “Trustworthy and reliable AI needs more than just evidence that a model usually works,” Azizan says. “For high-stakes applications, you need guarantees about the properties that must always hold. In this work, we established one such guarantee: boundedness. Our broader goal is to make principles part of how AI models are built, not just how they are tested.”
authors: David Chandler | Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems
